label: SYNTHETIC READER: a test instrument, never a reader. Fictional; not evidence about the book; not readership.

findings.quote: so you can see how far into it each chapter is
findings.why: Chapters are promised before any chapter has been named, so the sentence points at structure the reader cannot yet use.

findings.quote: The setup, hours one to five: the empty project
findings.why: The four phases are listed like a report of the record, with no 'I' and no hindsight on what each phase felt like or why it matters.

findings.quote: the team alone, steady, every wake started by the clock
findings.why: 'Wake' is used here before it is explained, and the explanation only arrives in the tour's Stop 2.

findings.quote: nineteen hours in a row, grouped into the setup
findings.why: The figure line repeats the four phases and hour count that the paragraph above has just given.

findings.quote: Four stops. At each, one picture, a few lines from me, and one line from the agent
findings.why: Run of short sentences announcing the format; one longer sentence would carry it.

findings.quote: The deck is a website. Every one of its 58 beats is a page that moves
findings.why: Short declaratives in a row; also 58 beats is stated with no hint of where a reader could check it.

findings.quote: built from the members' status files and wake records, not typed by anyone
findings.why: The Conductor's line two lines later says the same thing (the page shows what the files say), so the point is told twice.

findings.quote: a **wake** is one turn of work by one agent
findings.why: Key terms are defined after Stop 2 has already used wake, conductor and hold, and Stop 1 and 'five steps' at line 53 are never explained.

findings.quote: most of them read the same way: plan, go, done, clean, as planned
findings.why: As a source-minded reader I want to know who judged 'clean', and whether the editor ever refused a plan; the signature as control is not shown here.

findings.quote: Read in order, they are the team talking.
findings.why: It instructs the reader how to read; the thought could be offered as what the narrator found when reading them.

findings.quote: That list is often shorter than you expect
findings.why: Predicts the reader's expectation and ranks it as wrong.

findings.quote: you met them, and the ones who came after, in chapter 21
findings.why: A cross-reference to a chapter I have not reached is offered as something already done; a first reader has met no one yet.

findings.quote: And the historian made an error, and caught it itself.
findings.why: For a reader who prizes sources this is the most interesting failure, and it is given one clause with no what, which claim, or who signed the correction.

findings.quote: I left the times out of this page on purpose.
findings.why: The page asks to be checked and then withholds the evidence it points to; I cannot tell whether the repository is public or where the record lives.

findings.quote: I gave them the plan that same morning, and before noon the first draft
findings.why: This is a chronicle of events with no hindsight from the editor on what signing the plan meant or whether he rubber-stamped it.

what_holds: 03-the-tour.md: each stop pairs a concrete page with one agent line, and the 162 versus 163 wake count is surfaced and resolved in favour of the register, which is exactly the source discipline I want.
03-the-tour.md: the 'Dramatised' marking is honest about which words are invented and which pages are the record.

94-the-making-of-this-book.md: it names real failures (a hold written on a member's own judgement, the usage-limit evening, the historian's error) and says only the editor lifted the hold, which answers my worry about a rubber-stamping editor.
notes: Only the printed lines were judged; the team's notes were skipped. As a would-be newsroom builder I finish the tour wanting to know which role I would start with, and the making-of lists the members without saying what each does.
